parts.title: A summer on my uncle's farm
parts.instructions: Read the article and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
Last summer, I spent a month on my uncle's farm in the north of England. I live in a big city, and I had never seen a cow up close, so I was both excited and nervous.

My uncle gets up at five every morning, and on the first day, he woke me too. "Farm animals do not wait for anyone," he said. We fed the hens, collected eggs and milked the cows. The milk was warm, and my hands were so cold that I could hardly feel it. After a week, though, I was getting quite fast.

My favourite job was looking after the lambs. One of them, which I called Pepper, would follow me everywhere. When I left at the end of the month, I almost cried. My aunt said that Pepper looked for me in the field for three days.

The farm taught me many things. I learned that food does not come from a shop, but from hard work by people who get up very early. At home now, I try not to waste anything. And I have already asked my parents if I can go back next summer.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel before the visit?
options: Shy but very sure of herself
questions.explanation: She was both excited and nervous.

questions.prompt: What did the writer find difficult at first?
options: Finding a way round the farm
Learning the names of the animals
questions.explanation: The milk was warm, but her hands were so cold that she could hardly feel it.

questions.explanation: Pepper was one of the lambs that followed her everywhere.

questions.prompt: What did Pepper do after the writer left?
options: It looked for her in the field
It followed her car down the road
It did not eat for a week
It stayed in the barn for days
questions.explanation: Pepper looked for her in the field for three days.

questions.prompt: What did the writer learn from the farm?
options: Country life is boring for children
City food is better than farm food
Farm work is hard and starts very early
questions.explanation: Food comes from hard work by people who get up very early.

parts.title: A day in the life of a farmer
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There are three extra sentences.
parts.passage:
Tom Hayes is a dairy farmer, and he looks after a hundred and twenty cows. His working day begins at half past four, when it is still dark. [1] He puts on his boots and walks across the yard to the milking shed.

The cows are milked twice a day, once in the morning and once in the evening. [2] This takes about two hours, and he does it with the help of two workers.

After breakfast, Tom checks the fields. [3] In summer, the cows eat the green grass outside, but in winter, they stay in the barn and eat hay.

In the afternoon, there is paperwork to do. [4] He must also keep a record of every animal on the farm, which is a legal rule.

In the evening, the milking begins again. [5] He is usually in bed by nine, because the next day starts just as early.
sentences: Their new tractor cost more than the farmhouse.
His wife, who is a teacher, helps him with this work at weekends.
Modern machines make the job much easier than it used to be.
He makes himself a cup of tea first and checks the weather.
Most farmers do not take any holiday because the cows need milking every day.
He often says that he is a tired man, but a very happy one.
The calves are fed with a bottle three times a day.
He needs to be sure that there is enough food for the animals.

gaps.explanation: Making tea and checking the weather follows the early start and leads to putting on his boots.
Modern machines make milking easier, and the next sentence says it takes about two hours.
Being sure there is enough food connects to the cows eating grass or hay.
His wife helps with the paperwork, and the next sentence mentions the records.
Saying he is tired but happy follows the evening milking and leads to bed by nine.

parts.title: Country or city?
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage: Some people say that life in the country is better than life in the city. In the country, the air is cleaner, and there is [1] noise. You can see the stars at night, and neighbours often know each other well. However, there are also problems. Buses are not very frequent, [2] you usually need a car. Shops can be far away, and there may be no cinema. Young people [3] sometimes feel that there is nothing to do. In a city, on the other hand, you can [4] a job more easily, and there are lots of things to do. But the streets are busy, and everything is expensive. In the end, it depends on [5] kind of person you are, and on what you want from life. Many people try both before they decide [6] they prefer.

gaps.explanation: There is less noise in the country: a smaller amount.
Buses are not frequent, so you usually need a car: result.
Young people may feel that there is nothing to do: possibility.
You can find a job more easily in a city.
What kind of person you are: an indirect question phrase.
Decide which they prefer: a choice between two things.

parts.title: Short conversations
parts.instructions: Listen to seven short conversations. Choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: How early do you get up on the farm these days, Fadila?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: In the old days I got up at six, but now with the new cows I have to start at half past five, just before the milking machine starts.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s early.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Last year I got up at a quarter to six, and I was late every day. My husband still sleeps until six, then he makes breakfast. But my alarm rings at half past five now, and I’m used to it.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’d never do that.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You get used to everything.

question.prompt: When does the woman get up now?
question.explanation: Six was her old time and a quarter to six was last year’s; her alarm now rings at half past five.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Welcome to the hen house, everyone. We have fifty hens, so you might think we collect fifty eggs every day, but it doesn’t work like that. In spring and summer we sometimes get thirty, when the days are long and warm. Right now, though, it’s cold and the days are short, so we only collect about twenty each morning. We sell them at the gate, with the date on every box. If you’d like to see the hens, stay behind the red line and please don’t touch them or feed them with your own bread. They have a special food. Ask me anything.

question.prompt: How many eggs do the hens lay each day at this time of year?
question.explanation: Fifty is the number of hens and thirty is for spring and summer; now it is cold, so only about twenty eggs a day.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Frida, can I borrow your tractor today? Mine won’t start.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Oh, it’s not in the garage. I nearly put it there last night, but I was too tired.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Then it’s in the field behind the house?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: It was there on Monday. But on Tuesday my neighbour’s tractor broke down, so I lent him mine. It’s still on his farm. Ask him, he’s called Mr Hall and he lives next to the church.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Thanks, I’ll go there now.

question.prompt: Where is the woman's tractor today?
question.explanation: She nearly parked it in the garage and it was in the field on Monday; she then lent it to her neighbour, who still has it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Attention, drivers on the Elm Road. Please slow down, because there are about fifty sheep on the road near the farm. Some of you called to ask if the farmer is moving them to a new field. That’s not the case, he moved them last week. And it’s a clear morning, so nobody has lost their way in the fog. The sheep are out because a walker left the gate open at about seven o’clock and didn’t close it. The farmer and two police officers are bringing them back now. It should take about an hour. Thank you for your patience.

question.prompt: Why are the sheep on the road?
options: They are being moved to a new field
They are lost in the fog
question.explanation: He moved them last week and the morning is clear; a walker left the gate open.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Is it quiet in the village, Fran? You lived in the city for years.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Very quiet. I thought I’d miss the noise of the traffic, but I sleep better now. And the shops? There’s one in the village, and an online supermarket, so I don’t miss them much.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So what’s hard?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The people. I had friends there, we met every Friday for dinner. Here I don’t know anyone yet, but I’m joining the choir next week.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That will help.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I hope so. I call my best friend every evening.

question.prompt: What does the woman miss about the city?
question.explanation: She sleeps better without traffic and uses an online supermarket; what is hard is having no friends nearby.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Hello Jess, it’s Fitz. You asked where you can buy my honey. Last year it was in the village shop, but the shop closed in January, so that’s no longer possible. I nearly put a table at the end of the road, near the bus stop, because many people walk past, but the cars go too fast there and it isn’t safe. So now I’m beside the church, in the little garden by the gate. It’s open on Saturday mornings from nine until twelve. A jar costs four pounds, or you can buy three for ten. Come and try it, and say hello. Bye.

question.prompt: Where can people buy the honey now?
options: At the end of the road
question.explanation: The shop is closed and he nearly chose the end of the road but it is not safe; he now sells it in the garden beside the church.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Eudora, could you help me carry these boxes of apples to the van?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I’d love to, but I can’t. I’m not busy, the market is quiet today, and I’m not leaving until six. It’s my back. I hurt it on Sunday when I lifted a bag of feed.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Oh no. Did you see a doctor?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Yes, he said to rest for a week and not to carry anything heavy.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I’ll ask Tom then, or maybe Karl from the next farm.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Sorry. I can count the boxes and write the list, though.

question.prompt: Why can't the woman carry the boxes?
question.explanation: She is not busy and is not leaving until six; she hurt her back on Sunday.

parts.title: Understanding the main idea
parts.instructions: Listen to six short conversations and choose the best answer.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You look tired, Fabrice. Is farm work too hard?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: It’s hard, I’m up at five every day. But that’s not my problem. I got used to it a long time ago.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Are the animals making you nervous? I know the new bull is big.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: He’s fine, I’m not afraid of him. No, when I see the field of wheat in July, I think "I did that." My grandfather planted this farm, and I’m keeping it alive. I wouldn’t change it for any job.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s lovely. Your grandfather would be proud of you.

question.prompt: How does the man feel about his work on the farm?
question.explanation: He is used to the hours and not afraid of the bull; seeing the wheat makes him proud.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: We can’t carry on like this, Faustine. Fruit is rotting because nobody has time to pick it.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Agreed. The same three of us work twelve hours.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Should we open the shop on Sundays? Tourists come then.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s your idea, but I think we’re too busy already. A seventh day would kill us.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Fine. And the prices? Should we put them up?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Maybe next year. Not now.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: So we need people to help us.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Yes, two more at least, and we should ask in the village school too.

question.prompt: What do the two speakers agree about?
options: The shop should open on Sundays
The prices should go up now
question.explanation: She rejects Sunday opening and prices can wait until next year; both say they need two more people to help.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Did you hear, Filip? My cow won first prize at the county show!

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: That’s wonderful, Fadila! Well done!

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Thanks. I thought you’d be a bit upset, because your cow came second last year.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Honestly, no. I’ve won twice, so it’s your turn, and you have worked so hard. I’m happy for you. The only problem is that I’m exhausted, three days at the show, but I would go again tomorrow.

question.prompt: How does the man feel about the woman's prize?
question.explanation: He is not upset about last year and, although he is exhausted, he would go again; he is happy for her.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Have you seen the prices at the farm shop? A kilo of potatoes is now two pounds.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I know. People complain, but I don’t think they’re too high. The supermarket charges the same and the farm food is better.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: But they change every week. Last Monday it was one pound eighty.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: That’s my problem. I never know what to expect. If they could keep the same price for a month, I would be happy.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I agree. I’d buy more if I could plan my week.

question.prompt: What is the woman's opinion of the farm shop's prices?
question.explanation: She says the price is fair compared with the supermarket; her complaint is that it changes every week.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Ferran, I’d like to buy one of your goats.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Goats? Not yet. Come here first and let me show you how to milk her. It takes some practice, so I’ll do it slowly. Put your hand here.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I thought you wanted to sell her today.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: No, I want you to learn first. And I don’t need advice, I’ve kept goats for twenty years. Do it like this.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Oh, it’s harder than it looks!

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: You’ll get it. Try again, and hold her leg gently, so that she doesn’t move.

question.prompt: Why does the woman show the man how to milk a goat?
question.explanation: She does not sell the goat yet and does not need advice; she wants him to learn first.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: Frida, I’ve lost six chickens in one night.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Is it a disease? My hens were ill last winter.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: No, they’re healthy. And the fence is fine, I mended it in May.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Then what?

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: A fox. I found a hole under the door of the hen house. It must have dug in.

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Oh no. Put a stone in front of the hole.

turns.speaker: m
turns.text: I will tonight. I’ll also sit and watch with a torch for a few hours, in case it comes back.

options: A fox got into the hen house
question.explanation: The chickens are healthy and the fence is mended; there is a hole under the door where a fox got in.

parts.title: A talk about a dairy farm
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note. Write one or two words, a number, a date or a time.

turns.speaker: henrietta
turns.text: Good afternoon, everybody, and welcome to Hill End Farm. My family has lived here for over a hundred years. Today, we have eighty cows, although my grandfather started with only twelve. When I was a child there were about sixty, and the number has grown slowly. Each cow gives about twenty-five litres of milk a day. Some farms have cows that give thirty, but ours are a different type, and they live a calm life outside. Every second morning, a lorry comes to collect the milk. It used to come every day, but now we have a bigger cold tank. The lorry arrives at six, so we start work in the dark, even in winter, and the driver always has a cup of tea with us before he leaves. Let me introduce a few animals. The oldest cow is Daisy, she is seventeen years old, which is very old for a cow, and she wears a bell. The youngest are Rosie, Bella and Maple, but Daisy is the boss of the group. Now, the calves. People think they’re born in winter, but they’re born in spring, in March and April, when the grass starts to grow. In summer you can see them playing in the green fields, and the children on our tours love to give them names. After the tour, don’t miss the farm shop. We sell eggs and cheese and butter, and for children there is ice cream, made with our own milk. We make it in five flavours, and chocolate is the favourite. The shop is open until five. Please remember, don’t feed the animals, wash your hands afterwards, and keep children near the adults, because the floor can be slippery and the cows are bigger than they look. If you have any questions, ask me or one of the workers in the green jackets. Thank you, and enjoy the visit.

gaps.prompt: The number of cows on the farm today
gaps.explanation: The grandfather started with twelve and there were about sixty years ago; today there are eighty.

gaps.prompt: How much milk each cow gives every day, in litres
gaps.explanation: Some farms have cows that give thirty, but here each cow gives about twenty-five.

gaps.prompt: The milk lorry visits the farm on every ___ morning
gaps.explanation: It used to come every day, but now it comes every second morning.

gaps.prompt: The animal that is seventeen years old is called
gaps.explanation: Rosie, Bella and Maple are young; the oldest cow is Daisy.

gaps.prompt: Most calves arrive in the season of
gaps.explanation: People think the calves are born in winter, but they are born in spring.

gaps.prompt: A treat for children, made with the farm's own milk
gaps.explanation: Eggs, cheese and butter are also sold, but for children there is ice cream.

parts.title: An interview with a young farmer
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: Felipa, you’re only twenty-six and you run a farm. Why did you become a farmer?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: I didn’t plan it. I studied business, and after college I wanted to buy a small piece of land, but it was too expensive, so that was just a dream. And no, I didn’t win the farm in a competition, people always ask me that, ha! My grandfather got older and his back hurt, so he asked me to take over. I said yes in a minute, and the first year was very difficult, because I knew nothing about animals.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What is the biggest challenge for you?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: People say workers, and finding good ones is hard in summer, but I have a great team of five. Selling potatoes is easy, we have regular customers. The real problem is the weather. One storm in June can destroy a field, and you can’t do anything about it. I check the sky every hour. Last summer we lost half of the barley in one afternoon.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you sell at the market in June?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: June is a lovely month. Carrots are not ready until later in the summer, and onions we harvest in autumn, but the strawberries are perfect. People queue at my stall at eight in the morning for them. I sell out in two hours, and then I go home and sleep.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: And on Sunday afternoons, do you rest?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Mostly. The market is on Saturdays, not Sundays, so I don’t work all day. I do visit my grandfather sometimes, but he lives with my aunt now and they’re busy on Sundays. My favourite thing is a long walk with my dog, Tilly, in the hills. It’s my time to think, and the dog is very happy.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you enjoy most about the job?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: The money is not great, honestly. And I meet new customers every week, which is nice, but the best thing is to see my plants grow from tiny seeds into a green field. I feel proud every morning when I walk out of the house, and the evenings are the best, because the light is beautiful.

turns.speaker: i
turns.text: What do you say to young people who want to be farmers?

turns.speaker: f
turns.text: Be patient. Everything takes a long time, and the work is hard. I don’t think you should choose another job because of the money, you can earn more in an office, but you’d be less happy. And you needn’t wait until you’re older; I started at twenty-two.

questions.prompt: Why did Felipa become a farmer?
options: Her grandfather asked her to take over
She won a farm in a competition
questions.explanation: The land was too expensive and she did not win a competition; her grandfather asked her to take over.

questions.prompt: What is Felipa's biggest challenge?
questions.explanation: Workers are hard to find but she has a team, and potatoes are easy to sell; a storm can destroy a field.

questions.prompt: What does she sell at the market in June?
questions.explanation: Carrots are ready later and onions in autumn; in June she sells strawberries.

questions.prompt: What does she like doing on Sunday afternoons?
options: Working at the market all day
Visiting her grandfather at his home
questions.explanation: The market is on Saturdays and her grandfather is busy on Sundays; her favourite thing is a long walk with her dog.

questions.prompt: What does she enjoy most about the job?
questions.explanation: The money is not great and meeting customers is only nice; the best thing is to see her plants grow.

questions.prompt: What does Felipa say to young people?
options: Be patient and ready for hard work
Choose another job with more money
Wait until you are much older
questions.explanation: She says to be patient, that money should not decide, and that they do not need to wait until they are older.

parts.title: Getting to know you
parts.instructions: Answer each question in your own words. Aim to speak for 20-30 seconds.

questions.prompt: Have you ever been to a farm? What did you see there?
Do you like animals? Which ones?
